ChatGPT maker OpenAI is currently one of the most powerful companies in the world, and President Trump’s new AI Action Plan shows how eager each government is to persuade the tech company — and its competitors — to develop their tech on their soil.

The news: Trump unveils US AI Action Plan and signs three AI executive orders.

Why it matters: The 28-page ‘AI Action Plan’ aims to build out the country’s AI infrastructure, cement America’s dominance in the industry and prohibit all federal agencies from using AI contractors that don’t comply with the White House’s definition of “ideological neutrality”. The new policies reverse several Biden-era federal AI safeguards related to DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) and climate change, block state-level regulations on AI and further relax export rules so that global companies rely deeper on US-built AI. The move to get rid of existing AI regulations places further onus on individual companies to establish their own AI guardrails, especially if they operate across countries and jurisdictions. The US-centric policy also presents key challenges for fashion’s global supply chain and consumer base, which you can read more about here.

The news: OpenAI has shown some brands a pilot of a checkout feature that would enable users to complete purchases within its ChatGPT platform, according to a report by the Financial Times. It would charge brands commission for sales made this way.

Why it matters: When users search for products, ChatGPT currently shows recommendations with links to click through to brands’ own e-commerce sites. Bypassing this step opens up a clear revenue stream for OpenAI, but could significantly impact brands’ online sales. Those whose websites are picked up easier by ChatGPT would hold a significant advantage over those whose aren’t. No one’s quite sure what makes large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT tick yet, but there are some key practices emerging that could help brands optimise for AI search.

The news: WeTransfer has U-turned on plans to use UGC to train AI, after a revision in its terms of service caused widespread backlash.

Why it matters: Copyright protection has long been in place to safeguard creatives like photographers against their work being used without permission. Tech companies’ training of AI models on their work is proving a thorny issue within the fashion and creative industries, as it poses a risk of copies, duplication and direct competition — ultimately threatening their source of income. Given that WeTransfer is widely used within the creative industries, the company’s U-turn represents the perceived reputational risk that openly training AI models on creative work can cause.

The news: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said the company will build a data centre “the size of Manhattan” to fuel its planned development of AI products.

Why it matters: It’s the latest in a string of moves from Meta — which owns Instagram, Whatsapp and Facebook — that demonstrate the scale of the investment it’s making in developing AI products. Data centres are hugely expensive to build and maintain, and the size of what Zuckerberg is suggesting would cost billions of dollars. Zuckerberg has been very bullish on the potential for the company’s AI smart glasses in particular, and talk of Meta buying a stake in its Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses co-creator EssilorLuxottica has intensified in the last month.

#6694. Behold: Your Official ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Season 35 Cast Elimination Tracker

Get your dancing shoes ready, because season 35 of Dancing With the Stars is finally here! The reality dancing competition returned for a new season of live shows on September 15, and the show locked in some pretty major stars for the competition, from Olympian Amber Glenn to reality star Ciara Miller.

As always, this season of DWTS is pitting pop stars, reality show alums, actors, and professional athletes against one another in a heated classic ballroom competition. Each celeb is, of course, paired with a dance pro to guide them through their journey and help them get the biggest honor of all: the Mirrorball Trophy.

The entire season 35 cast was announced on Good Morning America on September 2, along with their professional partners, and here’s everything you need to know about the cast...including who has already been eliminated. (Side note: We’ll be keeping this updated each week, so check back to see who’s still in the competition.)

ABC always loves to throw an Olympian in the mix, and this season, it’s Blade Angel Amber, who revealed during an episode of House of Maher that “it’s been a dream of mine” to do DWTS “since I saw Meryl [Davis] do it in 2014.”

Dance experience: If you’ve seen Amber on the ice, then you know she’s a dancer at heart.

Last season, it was Alix Earle—but this season, the internet personality competing for the Mirrorball Trophy is Connor Wood, aka Fibula (who, btw, is good friends with DWTS alum Dylan Efron).

Known for: Brooke and Connor Make a Podcast and Fibs & Friends

Dance experience: If he has any, it’s news to me!

It wouldn’t be a season of DWTS without a few athletes, and in season 35, you can look forward to seeing two-time Paralympian Ezra Frech.

Known for: Tokyo 2020 Paralympics and Paris 2024 Paralympics (where he won two gold medals!)

Dance experience: He competes in track and field, but as far as I know, he’s new to the world of dance.

You know him for a million TV shows and movies, but did you know Harry was a professional dancer at the beginning of his career? Something tells us he’s still got it...

Known for: Glee, Shadowhunters, Grey’s Anatomy, and Crazy Rich Asians, among others

Dance experience: He served as a backup dancer for Beyoncé, Jennifer Lopez, Mariah Carey, and Madonna before transitioning to acting.

Maura was also rumored for months before her casting was announced. Back in March, she even told The Hollywood Reporter that DWTS would “be a huge challenge,” but one she was willing to take on. “I know I’d throw myself into it and all the looks and glitter,” she added.

Known for: Love Island UK, The Traitors, and Love Island USA: Aftersun

Dance experience: Maura told THR that she did “a bit of Irish dancing” when she was younger.

Big news for Fresh Prince fans, because Tatyana will be joining her onscreen big brother, DWTS host Alfonso Ribeiro, in the ballroom.

Known for: The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air and The Young and the Restless

Dance experience: While she’s better known for her singing skills, let’s not forget that we have her to thank for the TikTok dance trend set to Doechii’s “Anxiety.”

Jenna is stepping back into her dancing shoes! She started her career as a professional backup dancer before becoming an actor. But dancing has always been in her DNA, so we’re thrilled she’s back at it.

Known for: Step Up, Witches of East End, and The Rookie, among others

Dance experience: Where to begin! Jenna is an extremely experienced dancer and rose to fame thanks to Step Up. She was also a backup dancer for Janet Jackson.

She’s been in several iconic aughts movies, including Save the Last Dance. In fact, if she doesn’t recreate her dance from that movie, I will personally write a letter of complaint.

Dance experience: Once again: Save the Last Dance.

Along with an Olympian, most seasons of DWTS include a member of Bachelor Nation...and this season, it’s Tyler, who’s ready to compete six years after his ex, Hannah Brown, took first place in season 28.

Known for: The Bachelorette, Special Forces, and Going Home with Tyler Cameron

Dance experience: He competed on The Real Dirty Dancing back in 2022 (and finished as a runner-up!).

Back in December 2025, Jackson replied to a fan who asked whether he would “go on Dancing With the Stars next season” with a video compilation of dance clips, which he captioned, “Long story short... yes, yes I would.” Dreams do come true!

Known for: The Savannah Bananas baseball team and TikTok

Dance experience: Though he’s done plenty of choreography since joining the Savannah Bananas in 2022, Jackson surprisingly has no formal dance background.

As Jimmy Kimmel joked when his onscreen sidekick was announced: “Guillermo will become the first-ever parking lot security guard to dance with the stars.”

Known for: Jimmy Kimmel Live! (though he first rose to fame while working as a parking lot security guard at the Hollywood Boulevard Masonic Temple studio)

Dance experience: None that I know of, but I’m excited to see him bust out some moves!

Ciara was rumored to be joining the cast for season 34, but this year, it’s finally happening! As she told Us Weekly when the rumors first began, “I want [a pro] who is hard on me. Like, ‘You got to get this down.’”

Known for: Summer House, The Traitors, and Love Island USA: Aftersun

Dance experience: Ciara actually grew up dancing, and revealed to Us Weekly that she took ballet for 10 years.

Fans have been side-eyeing the middle Hanson brother ever since he showed up in the audience during season 34’s “Wicked Night” episode—and it seems that he is, indeed, hitting the stage this season.

Dance experience: Seeing as he spends most of his time behind the keyboard while performing, this is a little unclear.

Any Food Network fans here? Then you’re well aware of Giada, who’s been a household name for decades.

Known for: Giada at Home (among many other Food Network shows)

Dance experience: Unclear, but I’m excited to see what moves she might have!

Brooks Nader’s sister is following in her footsteps and we can’t wait!

Dance experience: TBD, but we’ll find out!

After cheering on his wife Whitney Leavitt during season 34, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives fan fave is now stepping into the ballroom himself (though let’s not forget that he already took the stage last year during Whitney’s Dedication Night dance).

Known for: The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives

Dance experience: Aside from doing TikTok dances, Conner appeared in the Off-Broadway dance show 11 to Midnight.

#6691. Andrew Scott On the Real-Life Story Behind His Heartbreaking Performance in Elsinore

In the fourth scene of the fourth act of Hamlet, our melancholy hero stands on a desolate Danish plain watching a Norwegian army march into Poland on a trivial errand. Turning to the audience, in the last of his soliloquies, he imagines “the imminent death of twenty thousand men that for a fantasy and trick of fame go to their graves like beds.”

How must it have felt for Ian Charleson, the sandy-​haired Scottish actor who rose to international stardom in Chariots of Fire but was dying of AIDS by the time he played his own legendary Hamlet at London’s National Theatre in 1989, to utter those lines? A silent, unjust war raged around him, as young men all over London were dying in isolation, their sheets burned as soon as their bodies were carted out, or, if they were lucky, driven home to take their final breaths in their childhood beds, eliciting whispers from the neighbors.

There is no way to know whether Hamlet, a role steeped in questions about life and death, was ever before played by a man who understood that his own death was so close. Those extraordinary circumstances are what animate Elsinore, the new film directed by Simon Stone that revisits and rejoices in Charleson’s final months. Many great actors have described their art as a means of escape—from the humdrum of reality, from the cage of the self. Andrew Scott, the Irish actor who is playing Charleson in Elsinore to a degree of fanfare approaching Oscar preordainment, does not share this view. Nor, he suspects, did Ian Charleson.

“The more I act,” Scott tells me from the quietest recess of a West Hollywood hotel restaurant on a 100-degree October day, “the more I see it not as pretending to be someone else but as exploring different parts of myself. Who would I be if I was born in this era or in this body or in this set of circumstances? A great actor once said that acting is an escape from acting. I think there’s a lot of sense in that.”

Scott, who turned 50 last month, grew up in Dublin in the shadow of the AIDS crisis and, like so many gay men of his age, has often thought how lucky he is to have been born just a few years later than the generation that died en masse. With better education and better treatment, men of his era survived, but for them sex and death could never be wholly disentangled.

“The fact that the current generation of young gay people feels a freedom from that is wonderful,” Scott says. He began his professional stage career at the Abbey Theatre in Dublin, in 1996, and he remembers what he calls “a conspiracy of silence around sexuality” at the time, a carryover from the beginning of the crisis when governments refused to speak or act. Elsinore revives not only the National Theatre of the 1980s but also the gay bars and cruising grounds of Hampstead Heath, where the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, a group of activists who dressed as Catholic nuns, educated gay men on safe practices at a time of governmental neglect. “People would ask them, ‘What do we do? How do we protect ourselves?’ ” says Scott, who learned more about Charleson and his era from his friend Stephen Beresford’s rigorously researched script. “Because there was no information, no help, all this silence. The terror of that silence is the thing that offends. That should be where the shame lies.”

Though Scott found mainstream success on British TV shows such as Sherlock and Phoebe Waller-Bridge’s Fleabag—as the so-called Hot Priest—he has remained dedicated to the theater and just completed a two-week run of Simon Stephens’s 50-minute monologue Sea Wall in New York. (In fact the play’s 19 performances were filmed as part of an upcoming motion picture about the process of creating theater.) In recent years Scott has taken on a pair of haunted gay roles, in Netflix’s stylish retelling of the Ripley story and, opposite Paul Mescal, in 2023’s All of Us Strangers. And yet he is still the rare openly gay actor whose sexuality has been greeted with a collective shrug.

“Well, it isn’t very interesting,” he says, shaking his head. “What was so insidious was that Ian and his predecessors had something to contribute to the film and television industry but weren’t given the opportunities in the same way, or else they were given the opportunities but they were also given a sort of silent choice: You can have that, but you have to conceal a huge part of your identity in return, while their straight counterparts didn’t have to make that sacrifice. In fact that part of their identity was celebrated rather than concealed or derided. I do feel that the playing field is starting to level out. There’s that great expression that prejudice doesn’t survive proximity. If you see people, you become less frightened of them.”

FACE FORWARD “He has no shield,” says costar Olivia Colman of Scott. “An instant and direct route to any emotion. He is the most beautiful empath.” Dior jacket and collar.

In the film Charleson bemoans the fact that all anyone remembers of Chariots of Fire, which won best picture at 1982’s Academy Awards, is the theme music. For those who came up in London’s theater scene when he did, the telling of his story feels overdue. Charleson was, by all accounts, a beloved figure in his artistic circle: clever and churlish, an excellent dancer and singer, abundantly generous to young actors. Hilton McRae, a Scottish actor who first met Charleson as a fellow student at the University of Edinburgh and was a close friend throughout his life, has seen Elsinore three times. “Andrew is Ian Charleson,” he says. “There’s that same sense of mischief. That same wicked wit. And I think off-screen he’s got the same kind of Celtic integrity about how to run his life.”

McRae missed his old friend’s Hamlet because he was busy playing Macbeth in his hometown of Dundee. So for him the film has been an almost uncanny invitation to enter into Charleson’s mind at a crucial moment. “When he had to say the lines ‘we defy augury. There’s a special providence in the fall of a sparrow. If it be now, ’tis not to come; if it be not to come, it will be now; if it be not now, yet it will come. The readiness is all.’ How do you say these things knowing what’s coming? How much was he hoping, how much was he in a kind of denial? I saw him when he’d finished. I went round to look after him one day, and he had Much Ado About Nothing and King Lear by his bedside. He was looking at Benedick, and he was looking at Lear. He wanted to do them. The marvelous thing about this film is that it’s basically about how important art is.”

For Juliet Stevenson, who plays Gertrude, Hamlet’s mother, in Elsinore, making the film offered an almost mystic mix of art and memory. Stevenson starred in Hedda Gabler at the National Theatre at the very moment when Charleson played his Hamlet; the two plays were in repertory on the National’s main stage, the Olivier. Years later, in 2017, she played Gertrude when Andrew Scott took on the role of Hamlet in an acclaimed run in London’s West End. She first met Ian Charleson when she was 20 and newly out of the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art. An actor had broken her leg in a production of The Tempest at the Royal Shakespeare Company in Stratford-upon-Avon, and Stevenson joined the cast while they were in dress rehearsals. Charleson was Ariel, and she remembers seeing him suspended over the stage by wires singing “Full fathom five.”

Scott as Charleson in a still from Elsinore.

“He was very beautiful, very camp, very kind of golden,” she recalls. “It’s easy to sentimentalize people who die young, who have a story like Ian’s, but he really was adored. He was supremely witty, funny, naughty, and acerbic, but kind, generous. Men or women—we were all a little bit in love with him.” Stevenson will never forget the moment she greeted Charleson at the National in 1989, not having seen him since Stratford. “Backstage the National is a great big community. Every show shares the green room, the canteen, the corridors. I was in a crowded elevator, waiting before the doors shut, and I looked across this landing and saw Ian walking towards the bar. I said, ‘Hey, Ian! Hi!’ He turned and said, ‘Hi, Juliet!’ I said, ‘Welcome to the National. How are you doing?’ He said, ‘Well, they say I’m dying! Isn’t that crazy?’ I just kind of stared at him. And then the elevator doors shut. The young man who’d been trying to keep it secret saw me and launched that message across that landing with a kind of strange gaiety. But—he was playing Hamlet! He turned his suffering into art. I hope that doesn’t sound pretentious, but I do believe that’s what he did.”

The director Richard Eyre’s much-ballyhooed staging of Hamlet arrived at the National with Daniel Day-Lewis in the title role; the actor was making a sort of homecoming to the stage as a newly minted movie star. (He would go on to win an Oscar for his performance in My Left Foot the next year.) Day-Lewis’s Hamlet was perhaps doomed by unreasonably high expectations; he did not receive the expected raves, and in September 1989, in the middle of a scene in which the prince confronts his father’s ghost, he walked off the stage and out of the production. Day-Lewis has not performed onstage since that night.

If there’s something Eyre disputes in Elsinore, where he is played by the actor Johnny Flynn, it is the suggestion that he offered Charleson the opportunity to take over Hamlet with a kind of benevolent calm. Charleson had been a huge success as Sky Masterson in Eyre’s production of Guys and Dolls at the National in 1982, and Eyre regarded him as a hugely capable classical actor too. But casting him this time was fraught with danger. “It was unimaginably painful,” Eyre remembers. “Daniel was a very close friend, and it was a terrible shock when he dropped out. I made the decision to cast Ian with the knowledge that he was ill and in defiance of a lot of my colleagues, who thought I was making a big mistake. My character appears absolutely stoical and generous, but in reality I was a total mess.”

The film acknowledges Charleson’s reluctance to come out publicly and even, at first, to his Hamlet castmates. Ian McKellen had come out a year earlier, on a live BBC broadcast, in part to protest Section 28, a Thatcher-era law that banned schools from “intentionally promoting homosexuality.” Charleson, always out to his friends, felt that the circumstances of his career made public disclosure impossible. “McKellen went on to become this astonishing global movie star, but at the time he didn’t have a movie career to worry about,” Eyre explains. “Ian Charleson had starred in Chariots and had a significant presence in Gandhi. He was lined up to be the next Robert Redford. I think he would have matured into a real international film star. But interestingly, he wanted more to do theater. He thought being a movie star was slightly ridiculous, as of course it is.”

At a moment when many queer people in the United States feel less safe, and when American investment in combating HIV globally has evaporated with the dismantling of USAID, Elsinore has a sense of political urgency that its creators may not have envisioned for it. While Scott knows that the film does not depart wholly from the somber tenor of his recent screen roles, he plays Charleson for laughs because humor was his essential mode, and he regards his unlikely Hamlet—with its four thousand lines over four hours—as a herculean effort against all odds.

“In some ways my fear was that we would fetishize Ian’s death rather than celebrate his life,” Scott says. “And actually his decision to play Hamlet at the very end of his life, to nail his colors to the mast in that way, when time was running out, is so life-loving.” Margaret Johnson, the doctor who cared for Charleson in his final months and who spoke extensively with Stephen Beresford as he was researching the screenplay, remembered occasions when he would come to her office the morning after a performance looking especially beleaguered. “Not tonight,” she would tell him. He would acquiesce, but then Johnson would watch him out her office window hailing a cab to the National. “As he says, I’d rather die of Hamlet than of AIDS,” Scott adds, quoting his character. “That’s somebody who wants to live. That’s important for me to say.”

Olivia Colman, who plays Johnson in Elsinore, was drawn to the tension between her character’s responsibility for the preservation of life and Charleson’s wish to focus on joy, even if it cost him time. “Art and joy make life worth living. He really proved that,” she says. Colman, like Eyre, thinks Charleson would be proud of Scott’s portrayal. “Oh, Andrew! He has no shield. An instant and direct route to any emotion. He is the most beautiful empath, and because it’s real, he’s not acting. He’s being.”

Scott and his two siblings lost their mother in 2024, and he says that work has had a grounding effect in the aftermath. Hollywood actors often speak of the necessity to strike while the iron is hot, and if he has the glorious awards season that has been augured for him (Scott would be the first openly gay man to win an acting Oscar), he will have his pick of roles in 2027. But instead he would like to do less. “I think it’s time to get my work-life balance back a bit, to sort of smell the roses,” he says. He wouldn’t mind a romantic comedy, or even a musical. If Charleson had King Lear at his bedside, perhaps it was because he knew that dying young would prevent him from doing the thing great Shakespearean actors, such as John Gielgud and Laurence Olivier, do: play Hamlet in their relative youth and play Lear as they age. But for Scott, such ambitions are far from the mind.

#6687. All the Gifts GQ Editors Want This Holiday Season 2026

As the desk at GQ that handles all things shopping, the GQ Recommends team has developed a rather motley assortment of wants, needs, and highly specific desires. We have good taste, if I may say as much, and no shortage of opinions about what makes a thing worth owning. So this holiday season, I asked everyone to set aside the usual assignments and show me what's on their own wishlists. What follows is an eclectic grab bag of A1 gifts, straight from the folks who spend all year finding the good stuff.

Still got names to cross off? Peruse our gift guides and sign up for the GQ Recommends newsletter for more good stuff worth giving (or keeping).

Years after getting married, I can say with confidence that the best thing about marriage is my wife. But a close second is the set of Sabre Bistrot flatware we received off our registry. A pleasure to hold and behold. And now they make chopsticks, which is unfortunate news for someone afflicted with my particular strain of completism. I have no choice but to finish the set. —MN

I couldn’t in good conscience ask for everything I want from Camiel Fortgens, which is, uh, everything. But this heavy-knit beanie, with the melange yarn and signature raw edges, feels like a reasonable place to start. —MN

It's true, the best radio station on the internet deserves its own hardware. Made in collaboration with tech company Atonemo, this dedicated player has big, tactile buttons for tuning into NTS 1 and 2, a dial for wandering through the Infinite Mixtapes, and the ability to plug straight into my amp. I feel so alive, and I've never been more excited to turn a dial. —MN

Nosying around other people’s bookshelves is a favorite pastime, and I can think of only a few libraries I’d rather rifle through than Luis Barragan’s. I’ve made the pilgrimage to his home and studio in Mexico City, and this new book offers a new look at the peerless architect’s life and influences through the personal collection he kept on his shelves. —MN

You may already know that we love Lady White’s top-tier white T-shirts, but we’re also massive fans of their sweats, especially this superweight hoodie. And when they say superweight, they mean it. I’ve own the zip-up version, and it's basically a winter coat. This will become my dog-walking hoodie, my 6 A.M. stroll to the bodega hoodie, and the late-night walk back from the cinema hoodie. —JB

Back in high school, some homies and I thought of ourselves as future producers. The music was terrible and thankfully is lost in the ether somewhere on SoundCloud, but despite those early attempts, I still find sampling a fascinating part of music. It’s a way to shut off the brain and think about songs in a new way. I doubt the music will be any better than it was back in the day, but I’ll have fun acting like Jamie XX or Nicolas Jaar, at least. —JB

I’m a pen-and-paper guy. You will often catch me feverishly jotting down thoughts in the middle of a meeting. I’ve recently needed to retire my old Moleskine notebook and found myself doing a deep dive into reusable leather-bound book holders that you can treat like a modular journal. You can add in different types of notebooks, calendars, and daily planners—the possibilities are endless. —JB

There comes a time in every man's life when he fancies himself a barista and thinks he should dedicate some time to learning how to pull a damn good espresso. I am that man, and the delusions are more errant than you would expect. Because I drink so much coffee, I’ve convinced myself I might as well get good at making it. —JB

As much as I don’t want to admit that I overindex on outerwear, my closet tells the truth. It’s so full that I can’t even shift any of the hangers without taking one of them out first. But that won’t stop me from eyeing this gorgeous coat from Auralee. It’s everything I want in a coat: dramatically long, artfully faded, and a deep black colorway. Now I’ll just have to find a new coat rack. —GO

I saw this bad boy in a shop and was so drawn to it. The colors are just right, the size is great, and the material is ultra-sturdy, but on this day, the devil on my shoulder told me not to get it that day. I came to my senses and came back the next day only to find that the tote was sold out. Hence why I’ve got it on my wish list because I believe in second chances and miracles. —GO

This little thing is a clever ear warmer that can be worn as is or can be slipped over the bill of your favorite hat. It’s silly and weird and cool and totally unnecessary. And yet, I would not be mad if this made its way into my stocking. —GO

I’ve always wanted a true Neapolitan-style jacket and getting to try on some of Natalino’s pieces in person during a pop-up in NYC has only stoked the fire. From the hand-stitched entails to the soft shoulders to the absolutely supreme fit, there’s no better jacket in my mind. —GO

No, I am not a ne'er-do-well Italian playboy loath to step into a leadership position at my dad's sprawling imports company. Yes, I would like to dress like one. —AG

Leave it to the vintage fiends in Japan to turn up a version of JCPenney’s canonical Big Mac flannel—the greatest flannel ever made, FYI—that might actually be worth the asking price. —AG

Okay, okay, okay. Once the sticker shock has worn off, think about how good of a boy I’ve been this year… —AG

You could drop $100K on leg-lengthening surgery and then rebuild your jeans rotation from scratch. Or you could just buy La Botte Gardiane’s naturally height-enhancing boots, which look great with the jeans you already own. —AG

I used to question whether the Eadem hype was another fad born of bloated influencer budgets, but dude. This balm is legit. I want every single color. You should get this for your girl for the holidays. If you’re scared of picking colors for her, opt for “Butter Mochi” (clear! unscented!) or “Sakura Shaved Ice,” a light pink that complements nearly every lip combo under the sun. —MH

I was treating my guy to his first ever foray into Buck Mason when I clocked a store employee wearing the Roper Jean and immediately lost the plot RE: which T-shirt the boy was trying on next. The silhouette! The wash! The contrast stitching! The complimentary Buck Mason tailoring for my stubby little legs! A girl can dream. A girl is still dreaming. Someone please gift this to me. —MH

Confessions of an adult seasonal allergies sufferer: I open the windows to air out my apartment despite knowing that that’s just welcoming the allergens into my home. Practical people might say I should address the issue at the root, but where’s the whimsy in that? Wouldn’t capitalism prefer that I purchase a solution to my problem instead? —MH

It took only one year at GQ and one “welcome to the team” bottle of D.S.&Durga to turn me into a fragrance fiend. For my bank account’s sake, I made a No New Fragrances vow earlier this summer … but gifts don’t count as breaking that pledge. Also, I really need a winter scent; my beloved Eau Splendide is more of a summer gal. —MH

I already own a bottle of Naked Dance, and it’s dangerously close to empty, which is the highest compliment I can give a fragrance. Well, the second highest. The first is how often I’m asked what fragrance I’m wearing, and I’m not ready to give that up. It’s a cult pick from a tiny niche house, right down to the cap, which is handmade from wood scraps and resin, exactly the kind of detail I can’t resist. —AH

I’m a vintage obsessive at heart, and this bracelet has that worn-in, one-of-a-kind look I’m always drawn to. Pyrite is also known as fool’s gold, and frankly, I’d be a fool not to want it. —AH

A good belt is the most underrated piece in any outfit, and my studded belt collection could always use one more. I’ve reached the point where I pick my outfits around my belts, not the other way around, and this one already has a few looks planned. The most practical gift on my list? I think so. —AH

All fall I’ve been hunting for the perfect pair of cords, mostly because I’m notorious for wearing the same pants almost every day. These feel like they walked straight out of a ’70s record sleeve, with that soft, slouchy fit. They’d slot into my current wardrobe perfectly, and finally give my usual pair a break. —AH

I love a gift you can give and secretly steal for yourself. This bathrobe is a “thoughtfu” gift for your partner that you’ll get to commandeer when they’re not looking. Two for the price of one really. You’re welcome! —LP

It’s a cliché, but the best gifts are the ones you wouldn’t buy for yourself but desperately want. And who doesn’t want a chic, soft, luxurious, well-designed towel? No one, is the answer. Tekla has a knack for unexpected color combinations that should feel wrong but somehow feel so right (this pink and brown combo is excellent)—a mood booster for any bathroom. Oh, and they’re unisex, making them a handy option when you have a last-minute gift to give. —LP

There is a myth that shower gel, or “smellies” as we call them in the UK (I’m British), are thoughtless gifts. I disagree. A luxury shower gel will add a little something extra to your morning routine, or someone else’s, and is a crowd pleaser for secret santa. This specific wash I can attest also smells incredible. —LP

Last holiday season, I treated my mother to a pair of Jenni Kayne cashmere socks. Since then, she’s never looked back and now has an expectation that Christmas = cashmere. She deserves it, so I’m happy to oblige (I may as well buy myself a pair at the checkout whilst I’m at it). They make a great gift for anyone who loves a cozy weekend at home or wants something luxurious to slip into after a day of hiking or skiing (my personal favourite time to treat my feet). —LP

A couple of decades ago, Helmut Lang was the place to go for a more city-minded denim jacket. And while those pieces still do numbers on the second-hand market, I’ve always found them a touch too fitted. So imagine my relief to discover this roomier Kaptain Sunshine take, which still feels special (and office-appropriate) due to its pleats, dark color, and smart single pocket. —LC

As a teenager, I was completely taken by this scent. Then, throughout my twenties, I tried all of the nicher body washes I thought I was meant to like. The ones that smelled like herb gardens, cedar forests, or sometimes… nothing at all. But following a recent, delayed flight-induced spin around Duty Free, I was reunited with Re-Charge Black Pepper. Please, kind gifters, reunite me with even more of it. —LC

#6685. Chic, Thoughtful Gifts That Will Delight the Woman Who Has Everything

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Spoil her with little luxuries she didn’t know she needed.

Shopping for the maximalist woman can feel trickier than shopping for anyone else on your list. Her beauty routine is set, her wardrobe is filled with pieces she adores, and her home is precisely curated. So how do you surprise someone who seems to have it all? As a maximalist with a circle of fellow maximalists, I’ve taken the guesswork out of it and rounded up presents she’ll be delighted to receive.

Look for thoughtful, personal gifts that won’t take up much space but will hold plenty of sentimental value, like a petite signet ring engraved with her initials, a silver frame holding a favorite photo of the two of you, or laundry detergent infused with her signature scent. Everyday luxuries are another lovely option, from an electric wine opener to ultra-cozy slippers or pajamas embroidered with her name. Ultimately, focus on meaningful little treasures or luxurious upgrades to the things she already uses and loves.

Ahead, discover the gifts she’ll remember long after unwrapping.

A dainty, personalized signet ring is sure to earn a permanent spot in her everyday jewelry stack. Choose from 14K yellow gold, sterling silver, or gold vermeil, and make it uniquely hers with an engraved monogram, initial, or meaningful date.

This hand soap smells divine and works like magic to whisk away lingering odors from garlic, onions, and the like, thanks to its gentle exfoliating beads. It’s quickly become a permanent fixture by my kitchen sink, and I haven’t looked back.

Bombas may be best known for its stylish, ultra-comfy socks, but the brand also knows a thing or two about making cozy slippers. And how sweet is this fleecy pair in a neutral check pattern? Whether she’s lounging around the house or stepping out for a quick errand, she’ll have a hard time taking them off.

With so much attention devoted to skin and hair care routines, lashes and brows often get overlooked. So why not treat her to Cécred’s cult-favorite Lash and Brow Builder, a little luxury she can easily incorporate into her daily beauty regimen.

Make the often-dreaded laundry routine feel a little more luxurious with detergent and dryer sheets that infuse her clothes with DedCool’s dreamy fragrance. With notes of bright bergamot, soft vanilla, and warm amber, the scent is reason enough to fall in love, but these laundry essentials go beyond smelling irresistible, helping lift stains and soften fabrics, too.

Eberjey is beloved for its buttery-soft pajama sets in the chicest colorways, and I’m a firm believer that one can never have too many pairs of luxurious PJs. Make her gift feel all the more special by adding a personalized monogram—complimentary, might I add.

There’s always room for another gorgeous pair of earrings in a jewelry lover’s collection, especially when they’re as exquisite as Fope’s designs. For a truly unforgettable gift, spoil her with the brand’s gold Prima earrings, embellished with glittering diamond accents.

Whether she loves hosting or just enjoys unwinding with a nice bottle of wine, an electric corkscrew makes opening her favorite vintage a breeze. No more struggling with a traditional bottle opener or wondering whether the screw is in far enough. Plus, it’s much easier on the wrists.

Elevate her winter wardrobe with an elegant, supremely soft cashmere poncho she can effortlessly slip on for an extra layer of warmth, whether she’s lounging at home, out and about, or braving the office air conditioning.

I’ve been raving about Gemi’s serum-infused hand sanitizers, which keep hands clean without leaving them feeling dry or stripped. This adorable keychain version clips right onto her handbag or keys for easy access, making it a practical yet charming gift for the woman on the go.

For a gift she’ll adore showing off on date nights and at glamorous evening affairs, look to couture designer Zuhair Murad’s new collaboration with footwear brand Aldo. Known for avant-garde creations and intricate embellishments, Zuhair Murad brings a couture-inspired touch to Aldo’s stylish, affordable designs in a collection of party-ready accessories. Not only are they dainty enough for everyday wear, but they’re also available in every birthstone, allowing you to personalize her pair with a gem that corresponds to her birth month—or simply choose her favorite stone.

If you’re looking to make a major impression, a designer handbag is a surefire way to earn yourself the title of her favorite gift-giver. Gucci is known for its sumptuous leather, and this understated shoulder bag is destined to become her new go-to for work and beyond.

A luxurious silver photo frame holding a cherished memory is a sentimental present she’ll be proud to display. For an extra-personal touch, have it engraved with a meaningful date, sweet message, or heartfelt sentiment.

#6684. This Couple Rented Out a 17th-Century Stone Village for Their Misty Cliffside Wedding in the Azores

Kathryn Mawhinney and Grayson Judge’s first date was technically a phone call. A seven-hour phone call, to be precise. “We both grew up in the Bay Area but didn’t meet until 2024,” says Kate, who at the time was still finishing college in Atlanta. Rather than waiting until they were in the same place, the two spent six weeks talking on the phone every day. “After that first call, I knew I needed to have her in my life,” recalls Grayson. “She was unbelievably charming, funny, and warm, and I knew there would be a line of guys waiting for her when she got home.”

When they eventually had their first in-person date, it was in San Francisco, halfway between their two hometowns. Grayson planned a night out at a tequila bar (margaritas are Kate’s favorite), followed by tapas for dinner, and finally a lookout point in the Russian Hill neighborhood. “I texted one of my buddies on my way home and told him I would marry her one day,” he says.

Fifteen months later, Grayson proposed at that same lookout point. “I got her there by convincing her we were on our way to brunch with my cousin, and instead brought her back to the place where it had all started,” he says. Despite the couple having previously talked about a general timeline for getting engaged, the actual proposal caught her off guard. “The second I realized what was happening, I immediately started sobbing uncontrollably,” she says.

When the couple was deciding where to get married, they landed on an intimate gathering of family and friends in Fajãzinha on Flores Island in the Azores. (They also plan to have a larger wedding next summer in a town the bride’s family grew up visiting.) The island is among the most remote in the Azores, and is where Grayson’s maternal ancestors are from. “My Azorean heritage has always been a source of pride for my family and me,” he says. “Returning to my ancestral homeland to marry the love of my life was truly an indescribable feeling.”

They rented out the entirety of Aldeia da Cuada, a 17th-century stone village turned hotel that was able to accommodate everyone in town for the week’s festivities. “The little houses were originally built higher on the island to escape pirates, and the whole place felt like a fairy tale,” Kate says.

Kate took the lead with conceptualizing and planning, while Grayson spearheaded logistics. “My man of honor jokes that it was really just me and my 100-page Canva board against the world,” she says. Kate sourced vendors from all over the world, including Etsy stationery artists and commercial wholesalers for embroidered towels and aprons.

Among their standout vendors was their florist, Alice of Jungle Utopia, who purchased special headphones that translated French to Portuguese so she could figure out how to import the flowers they wanted. “And on top of everything else, she even foraged in the mountains for garnishes for our Palomas. She is truly such an angel,” Kate says.

Carlota, the owner of Aldeia da Cuada, was also instrumental in the planning process. “She and her team went above and beyond, building cocktail tables by hand, learning to make passion-fruit margaritas on the fly, and working with civil and parish authorities to help pull off the first wedding our church had hosted in more than 20 years,” Grayson says. “I joke that Carlota is the second love of my life,” Kate adds. “We truly could not have pulled this off without her.” A month before the wedding, they also brought on a team of two from Mason Market (Sam and Tyler) to bring everything over the finish line.

For their welcome party, Kate chose a Ralph Lauren gown circa 2001 (her birth year) and paired it with Jimmy Choo heels and her mother-in-law’s diamond studs. “The earrings were especially meaningful: They had belonged to her mother and were originally given to her by Grayson’s late grandfather, whose ashes were scattered on Flores,” Kate says. Grayson opted for a dark brown suit and tonal shirt from Todd Snyder.

The morning of the wedding, Kate slipped into a robe and slip she had thrifted in France to get ready. “We didn’t have elaborate dressing teams or glam squads for everyone,” she says. “My best friends [got] ready on the floor using their iPhones as mirrors. They joked that they experienced the purest form of girlhood.”

The ceremony took place in the Church of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios, a Catholic church constructed in 1776. Kate walked down the aisle in a long-sleeved, open-back gown that she had found while shopping with her grandmother and mother. “We customized the Sareh Nouri gown extensively, removing the bow and extra train in the back, changing the short sleeves to long sleeves, extending the train, and adding tiny buttons along the sleeves,” she says. She paired the gown with Amina Muaddi heels, vintage earrings, and a veil with a removable blusher.

“I will never forget the first glimpse I caught of her through a small crack in the wooden church doors,” Grayson says of Kate’s dress. For his own look, he wore a Saint Laurent tuxedo with a Giorgio Armani tuxedo shirt, which had been gifted to him by his mother-in-law a few years earlier.

A local priest named Júlio presided over the ceremony, which was half in English and half in Portuguese. A few of the townspeople sat in the back pews to witness the ceremony. “There was something so moving about having them there,” Kate says. “It made me feel like we were becoming part of something much bigger than just our own marriage.

After the ceremony, the two were waiting to sign the marriage certificate when Kate felt a light tap on her arm. “I looked down, and a little girl handed me a drawing and said, ‘This is for you,’” she recalls. It was a picture she had drawn of the couple. “It was the pianist’s daughter, and we were told later that it was her first wedding and she thought that Kate was a princess,” Grayson says.

The group proceeded down to the town square of Fajãzinha, where a wine bar had been set up. “Each guest had a wine glass with a Portuguese scarf tied around it, which Kate had embroidered with their names,” Grayson says. The priest, local townspeople, taxi drivers, and shepherds all joined the celebration.

When guests arrived at the reception, a handwritten letter from Kate awaited each of them at their respective place settings. “Kate is the only person I know who would handwrite four-plus-page, personal, heartfelt letters to 29 people expressing her gratitude for their role in helping her become the woman she is today,” Grayson says.

Once speeches kicked off, the couple were both brought to tears when Grayson’s mother took the microphone. “She hired a genealogist and began the speech by reading the names of Grayson’s ancestors who had lived on Flores, including multiple couples who had been married in the very same church where we had said our vows just hours earlier,” Kate says. “We had no idea, and it made the entire day feel even more special.”

The group eventually migrated to the circular stone roof of an old atafona (traditional mill) and danced under string lights, drank wine straight from the bottles, and partied into the night on the makeshift dance floor (“with a constant fight for who was on aux”). The after-party moved to the pool, where everyone swam and danced until 6:30 in the morning. “As proof that I was having the best night of my life, I managed to roll my ankle and just kept dancing,” Kate says.

Looking back, it was these moments of friendship and family they say they’ll remember most. “I think an underrated part of a wedding is that while you’re marrying the love of your life, you’re surrounded by the people who were your entire life first,” Kate says. “One of my relatives, who hadn’t flown in decades because he was afraid of flying, got on a plane because I was getting married. My mom pressed three of the groomsmen’s suits when they wandered into her little stone house looking for help… They say your wedding sets the tone for your marriage, but I hope that week sets the tone for the rest of our lives.”

Flores Island. In the foreground is the historic stone village of Aldeia da Cuada, where we held our reception, and in the distance, Fajãzinha village and the Church of Nossa Senhora dos Remédios. The last time a member of my family was married in that church was 150 years ago. —Grayson

#6682. RIP to LIV, the Golf League No One Ever Really Cared About

The most remarkable thing about the era of LIV Golf, a five-year run characterized by near-parodic blunders and missteps, is that leadership and its public-facing talent don’t appear to have learned any lessons from their many failures.

From the beginning, the upstart league, established in 2021 as a rival to the dominant PGA Tour, was plagued by its own ineptitude. It’s only fitting—after LIV’s newfound lifeline, private investment firm BC Partners, reneged on a $300 million investment—that the brand’s figureheads are now celebrating the end by taking a victory lap. Tone-deaf doesn’t begin to describe it.

LIV CEO Scott O’Neil—who took over for original boss and Major winner Greg Norman in January of 2025 and was faced with finding new cash flow after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund announced in April that it would no longer finance the operation—clearly exists in a different reality than our own. “Together, our team delivered world-class individual and team competitions across five continents, built a global business, secured pathways to The Open and U.S. Open… and built a league capable of attracting both elite and rising talent from around the world,” he said in a statement late last week. It’s unclear if the farewell tour will continue, though, an even newer report suggests that BC is looking to purchase a bankruptcy loan from LIV’s current owners. If this Hail Mary works, LIV’s future would look much different than the one O’Neil has promised.

Another way to look at it? One of LIV’s biggest accomplishments was that the league, despite its intentions to diversify the game and bring fun back into a sport that had come to personify privilege and exclusivity, inadvertently consolidated the PGA Tour’s power as a monopolistic behemoth now primed to solidify its status as the only league in town. They helped usher in a new era of leadership and investment for the Tour, including the introduction of CEO Brian Rolapp, who is by all accounts the most well-liked and accomplished boss it’s had in quite some time.

LIV also managed to tarnish the reputations of its biggest stars. Jon Rahm, who was vehemently opposed to the dog and pony show when it was announced, only to sheepishly take a bag of blood money so big his great grandchildren will never have to work a day in their lives, is now one of the game’s great “What If?” stories. Prior to the US Open at Brookline Country Club in June 2022, the defending champion was asked about his thoughts on the upstart league. “Money is great,” he said. But Rahm and his wife thought about it further. “Will our lifestyle change if I got $400 million? No, it will not change one bit.” Just over a year later, he defected to LIV.

Then there’s Phil Mickelson, who was poised to become a fixture of the American Ryder Cup team and widely considered a shoo-in to hold a cushy job as an analyst for golf’s biggest broadcasting events. Upon joining the league, he admitted in a conversation with Alan Shipnuck that Saudi Arabia was a terrible bedfellow. (Shipnuck and Mickelson have disagreed over whether the comments were on or off the record.) “They killed Khashoggi and have a horrible record on human rights. They execute people over there for being gay,” he explained. But there was a caveat: LIV was simply a “once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to reshape how the PGA Tour operates.” Miraculously, he got that part right.

Prize money on the PGA Tour is greater than ever, the Tour’s main events have recalibrated, and its season-ending championship series has been completely reimagined. Mickelson won’t be allowed within 100 miles of it.

The league’s biggest attraction, Bryson DeChambeau, is theoretically the worst-situated of the game’s many turncoats, though he’s probably more excited about growing his YouTube channel than he is about playing golf anyway. No one’s put their reputation on the line for this gaggle of buffoons quite like DeChambeau, who spoke proudly about how LIV was “growing the game” and “bringing team golf to the world.” This past weekend, he shared a statement on the dissolution of LIV. “I still believe in team golf,” he wrote. “It may look different in the future, but I still believe it’s essential to growing the game.” A loyal foot soldier, even from the grave.

It was always about the money. Nothing more, nothing less. This was a cash grab of epic proportions, and golfers not good enough to earn their keep on the PGA Tour took a life raft and briefly found themselves in possession of luxury superyachts. Then, low tide left them holding bags of cash and not much else. Was it worth it? For most of these golfers, probably. They were past their primes when LIV began; they’re still past the primes now, and just a helluva lot richer.

The league positioned itself as a disruptor, and disrupted so poorly that they’ve turned the PGA Tour into the strongest version of itself we’ve seen since Tiger Woods was at his peak. All that bloviating about the good of LIV Golf from its loudest talking heads is a bunch of nonsense.

It’s hard to tell if these statements are one last line of defense or more genuine delusion from LIV’s last advocates. They came in with the idea of sticking it to the PGA Tour, which at the time was facing bleak circumstances, bogged down in nonsense before redirecting its energy towards batting this gnat into extinction. Ultimately, LIV helped the PGA Tour save itself.

Now it’s gone for good, and five billion dollars later, we’re not gonna remember a damn thing about it. Not the players, not the leadership, and surely not all the ways they supposedly grew the game while merely growing their own bank accounts.

#6678. Louise Kennedy on Her Sweeping Second Novel, ‘Stations’

At 59, the Irish novelist Louise Kennedy is the literary world’s latest great find. She’s also her own self-discovery project: After working as a chef for nearly 30 years, Kennedy was in her late 40s when she first tried to write fiction.

She’s since set raw-hearted and tragically romantic tales in the shadow of the Troubles, the decades-long political conflict in Northern Ireland. Sexual and political awakenings exist side by side in Kennedy country. Trespasses (2023), her debut novel about a Catholic-Protestant love affair in 1970s Belfast, was translated into more than 20 languages and made into a miniseries starring Gillian Anderson Anderson. Her follow-up novel, Stations, published this month, is a punkier and even more electric work. It opens with Róisín, a bolshy and unpopular teenager, striking up a friendship with Red, a troubled local boy from a wealthy family. The story then jumps-cuts into the future, where Róisín finds Red living in a London squat, and arcs all the way into midlife.

Kennedy spoke to Vogue over Zoom from her home in Sligo about being a late bloomer, Irish-granny maximalism, and why the Troubles have been taking off.

Vogue: According to the lore, you didn’t write a word of fiction until you were 47.

Louise Kennedy: It’s true, I wasn’t scribbling away in secret. I didn’t write a thing until I joined a writing group, and even that was under duress. A friend who was involved when it was being set up kept messaging me all day, and I kept saying, “No, I’m not going.” I was busy, I was tired, and it was a ridiculous notion. I’m a cook. Why would I go to a writing group? Then she turned up at my house and told me to get in the car, so I went along. I’ve no idea why she did it.

I don’t think it was a bad thing to be older and trying to write. I couldn’t have done this in my 20s. I’d have been way too self-conscious, and I wouldn’t have had the discipline. And if, in the very unlikely event, I had managed to publish something and anybody liked it, I wouldn’t have been able to handle the attention. Not in any shape or form.

You talk about writing in a way that isn’t tortured. You can write thousands of words a day. Is that the chef in you?

I think maybe it is. I was a chef for nearly 30 years. We worked what were called split shifts but were really double shifts: in at 10 in the morning, still there at 11 at night, then out for a few drinks. The only break you’d get was sticking your head out the back door for a cigarette. So I tend not to feel sorry for myself about deadlines.

Writing from the point of view of a teenage girl seems to come easily to you. What were you like at that age?

I was awful. I was probably a bit like Róisín, fighting with everybody, really self-centered, really dramatic, deeply unpleasant a lot of the time. And I think, like her, I imagined there was some better, bigger life outside the place I’d ended up.

You don’t shy from portraying the horrors of alcoholism.

I was practically brought up in a bar. My family had a pub, and if there’s a lot of drinking, some people will become alcoholics. Three out of four of my grandparents were alcoholics, and I had uncles and aunts and neighbors who were, too. I went to London in the ’80s and lived in that precarious way; we were all out drinking cider and smoking and doing whatever else. A lot of us stopped and some of us didn’t. Even when we were 18, 19, 20, there were signs that some people were going at it harder than everybody else. Several of them are dead.

Nobody asks a child what they want to be and hears, “An alcoholic wrecking my home.” Nobody wants to end up like that. In the early days of surgery, before proper anesthesia, they poured whiskey down people’s necks before they amputated an arm or a leg. For a lot of people it’s still the acceptable form of painkilling.

In Trespasses, it was gutting to read about Cushla’s constant vigilance and anxiety where taking care of her mother, Gina, is concerned. How did Gillian Anderson end up playing Gina?

On publication day for Trespasses in the UK, in April 2022, there was a dinner, and I knew Gillian was going to be there. I was nervous so I drank too much. I was sitting beside her and she told me how much she loved the book, and how much she loved the character of Gina, the mother. Because I was a bit drunk, I thought it would be entirely reasonable to ask whether she’d play Gina in the adaptation. And Gillian said yes! I thought: This is fantastic. Then I woke up in the morning going, “Oh my God, what have you done?”

Róisín grows up to write about interior design for a living. How would you describe your own aesthetic?

Irish-granny maximalist. My house is full of stuff. I’m obsessed with old hot water bottles.

Why do you think American readers are so drawn to books about the Troubles right now?

I think a lot of it is about time. There were books published about the conflict in the ’70s and ’80s, and then it seemed to dry up. It had gone on for so long and became such a dirty conflict that maybe editors didn’t want to publish it, and maybe people didn’t want to read about it. More than 25 years have passed since the Good Friday Agreement, and I think it took that long before people were ready. I do think it was about trauma, and it needed to be put to bed for a while.

This conversation has been edited for clarity.

#6676. How Martine Rose Became Menswear’s Secret Weapon

After much speculation, the fashion rumors were true: Martine Rose is officially Balenciaga’s next creative director. It’s undoubtedly her biggest job yet—and a historic appointment: she is the first woman creative director to lead the French house. Rose succeeds Valentino vet Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose departure after just three seasons was announced yesterday. This is a major moment for the British-Jamaican designer, who has spent nearly two decades building a namesake label that wields outsize influence.

Rose has long occupied a curious position in menswear: a designer’s designer with a devoted following of both high-fashion heads and the streetwear obsessed. Since launching her eponymous brand in 2007, she’s developed an unmistakable visual language of playful styling, graphic-driven sportswear, offbeat tailoring, and covetable sneaker collabs. Her clothes take the familiar and make it strange, infusing everyday garments with humor, a touch of romance, and occasionally an ugly-chic sensibility: think square-toed loafers, chap-covered suit trousers, and soccer jerseys with lace-up fastenings. The results can be loud, wildly stylish, and routinely fun.

“I’ve always been drawn to the way men are told to dress,” the designer told GQ in 2023. She’s been on a mission to subvert those conventions ever since.

On the Martine Rose runway, sportswear and tailoring regularly share the spotlight. Much of that sensibility comes from her ability to borrow from and fuse London’s historic subcultures: ravers and club kids, football fanatics and nattily dressed mods. She tends to embrace the unusual and eccentric rather than focusing on making everything read as conventionally stylish. One look from a recent collection featured a swishy track jacket tucked into straight-leg blue jeans, and another paired a perfectly tailored coat with athletic shorts and knee-high socks. In Rose’s universe, there is no wrong way to mix and match. That’s part of her charm.

That sensibility eventually caught the eye of Demna during his decade-long tenure as Balenciaga’s creative director. The firebrand Georgian designer reached out to Rose in 2015, and she spent the next three years as a menswear consultant for the house during a high-profile era defined by supersized proportions and outlandish accessories. The blazers were big and the boots were bigger, but the star power of the celebrities who wore them was the biggest of all.

Rose is no stranger to dressing famous people. Her clothes have landed on some of the most photographed men in the world: Drake, Timothée Chalamet, Bad Bunny, A$AP Rocky. Perhaps her most visible endorsement came at the 2025 Super Bowl, when Kendrick Lamar strutted around the halftime show in a custom red, white, and blue leather varsity jacket designed by Rose. (In 2023, the rapper had boasted about how he wears “Martine when I board jets” on the Baby Keem track “The Hillbillies”; a year later, he sported several of her designs in his “Not Like Us” video.) Over the years, Rose has become one of the rare designers whose collections are covered by both Vogue and Hypebeast, a testament to her appeal across fashion’s various tribes. She’s been a fixture at London Fashion Week, and made her Milan debut in 2024. She has two hit Supreme collaborations under her belt. When Nike came calling, Rose produced remixed versions of the Shox (which Lamar wore while he accepted three Grammys in 2023) and Monarch sneakers—turning two of the Swoosh’s most divisive silhouettes into lustworthy objects. Tommy Hilfiger enlisted her for a collection centered on the streetwise style of Tommy Jeans in the ’90s. Brands know she can deliver the goods.

Which brings us back to the Balenciaga appointment. Rose obviously knows the house, or at least Demna’s vision for it—a vision that brought meme-worthy fashion but also massive creative and commercial success. A statement from Luca de Meo, CEO of Kering (the French luxury group that owns Balenciaga), included all the boilerplate press language about innovation, creativity, and culture. More crucially, Rose has proven she can make familiar clothes feel fresh, taking what guys are already wearing and turning them into something surprising and covetable. The question is now what Rose will be able to do with the resources of a global luxury powerhouse at her disposal. She’s spent much of her career building her own idiosyncratic world at Martine Rose. At Balenciaga, she’ll find herself on a much bigger stage with a vast audience and a completely new rulebook.

In 2020, when discussing her reputation as something of an underground darling, Rose told GQ: “I’ve never really wanted to be part of a big thing. Anything that is mainstream—since I was small—hasn’t really appealed to me.” Six years later, she’s earned one of the biggest jobs in fashion. There’s great fun in evolution, too.

#6674. In Her First-Ever Stand-Up Special, Janelle James Sees Through the Dark

In Janelle James: How Romantic, the Emmy-nominated actor and comedian gets right into it.

The hour opens with James’s take on American politics, from the physical attractiveness (or the lack thereof, as the case may be) of the GOP’s key operators to more pointed, cross-party digs at, say, Hunter Biden and Senator Mitch McConnell. (“He died four times. He died so much, it just became a thing.”) There isn’t much about Washington that she doesn’t find “weird.” (The special may have gone a little differently had she taped it after this month’s midterm elections.)

“The show is written in four chunks,” James explains over a Zoom call from Los Angeles on November 2. “My political segment, my fame segment, my dating segment, and a segment on violence—and I can switch them around at will. A day before taping, I thought, I’m going to open on politics and get that out of the way. On the road, actually, I was ending with it.”

James says she developed How Romantic over about 70 sets, with a break last year to film Season 6 of the hit television series Abbott Elementary, in which James plays the endlessly chaotic school principal Ava Coleman. “I built the hour somewhat in that first stretch,” she says. “It marinated in my brain when we went back to shooting. Then when we were on hiatus again, I went on a little mini tour, multiple weekends, Thursday to Sunday, often with double shows.”

James stresses that How Romantic is no “Abbott revue.” “This special is an introduction for a lot of people to me as a stand-up,” she says. A stand-up and, well, a real, raw person behind the outsized television personality. “I start the show out sitting down on purpose, so people get a sense of what the vibe is going to be. I’m not really loud. I’m not really doing act-outs. I don’t really have props. This is me performing as myself, and this is how it’s going to go,” she says. “Those who’ve been following me as a comedian since I started are like, ‘People have no idea how dark you are.’”

Asked whether Janelle and Ava have blended together as Abbott has gone on, James says: “There’s definitely more overlap now. I think that’s true for all of us [in the cast]. Some of the people in the writers’ room I’ve known for years. They know me as a comedian, to the point where I’m like, ‘I’m going to stop talking to y’all,’ because I’ll say something and it ends up in the show. A lot of my colloquialisms—Ava says ‘hot’ all the time. That’s something I say! And that messes with my brain sometimes.”

James’s own brand of humor leans sarcastic and cynical—even a little melancholy (“Everything is funny and nothing is funny,” she says early in the hour). It’s also more explicit than anything an ABC mockumentary sitcom would allow. Just take the sex act James simulates with a microphone. “That part didn’t come until one of my final shows [before the taping]. I just did it one night, offhand, with the club mic,” James says, grimacing. “We went the next day and got me my own, because I thought, I’m going to keep doing that.”

The divide between the version of herself that exists in the popular imagination and the one who shows up onstage in How Romantic feels to James related to the ongoing debate in Hollywood about how comedic performances are received and judged in comparison with dramatic ones.

“What people don’t think about, and the reason comedy is just as important as drama—and harder in certain instances—is that we are performing joy when our real lives can be falling apart,” James says. “I won a comedy contest the night my dad died. I’ve done many stand-up shows straight out of a break-up. That’s very hard to do. Because we make it look easy, people don’t rate it the same as crying on command. I can cry right now! I’m a world of sadness. But it’s about performing joy.”

#6672. No-Knead Pumpkin Focaccia

For those who fall into the pumpkin-should-be-savory camp, let us offer up a new recipe primed to become a seasonal staple: Pumpkin Focaccia. The iconic bread we know and love is ripe for the pumpkin treatment, lending it a golden hue and earthy sweetness. This version doesn’t require any kneading, making it straightforward enough to pull off in a single afternoon. You’ll perform a series of folds as it rises, simply pulling and stretching the dough to help it develop gluten. A showering of fresh rosemary and flaky salt on top is optional, but it takes crisp, plush focaccia from good to great. Serve it with a bowl of olive oil for dipping or a schmear of cream cheese to lean into the seasonal profile.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Mix one ¼-oz. envelope active dry yeast (about 2¼ tsp.), 5 cups (625 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, 1 Tbsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 Tbsp. light brown sugar, and 1½ cups warm water in a large bowl until a dry, shaggy dough forms. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot 15 minutes.

Place a small bowl of room-temperature water on work surface for easy reaching. Uncover dough and moisten hands in water, shaking off excess. Stretch 1 side of dough up and over to meet opposite side; turn bowl 90°. Repeat process 3 more times, turning bowl after each fold. (This constitutes 1 full fold.) If dough doesn’t always stretch to meet opposite side, just aim for the middle. Remoisten your hands and shake off excess water any time dough begins to feel sticky. Cover dough and let sit 30 minutes (set a timer). Repeat entire process 2 more times (folding and resting), about 1 hour more. By the last full fold, the dough should be significantly smoother and tighter.

Pour ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil into a 13x9" metal baking pan. Lightly oil your hands and punch down dough, then transfer to prepared pan. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Turn dough salted side down to coat both sides in oil. Press into an even layer with your fingers. Cover with plastic wrap and let sit in a warm spot until puffy, about 45 minutes.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 450°. Unwrap focaccia and scatter rosemary leaves and more sea salt over if desired; drizzle with oil. Oil your hands and press fingers into focaccia several times to create dimples across surface, making sure to press fingers all the way down to the bottom of the pan. Bake focaccia, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown, 23–28 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let focaccia cool slightly in pan. Using a metal spatula, turn out focaccia onto rack and let cool completely.

Do Ahead: Focaccia can be made 1 day ahead. Store tightly wrapped at room temperature.
