#6583. Jolie Made the Showerhead a Beauty Staple. What’s Next?

A showerhead is not an obvious candidate for brand cachet. Yet Jolie has turned one of the bathroom’s most overlooked fixtures into a beauty-wellness product and a conversation piece. Through Erewhon drink collaborations, a Copenhagen Fashion Week art installation, and “Shower Thoughts”, its interview series featuring creatives and designers, the brand has made a long-ignored item newly desirable.

Nearly five years after launching with a single filtered showerhead, Jolie co-founder and CEO Ryan Babenzien is ready for the brand’s next phase. The beauty and wellness company, which is on track to generate $65 million in revenue in 2026, is introducing its second product on November 11: the Filtered Handheld Showerhead. Available in five of the brand’s signature colorways, including Modern Chrome, Brushed Gold and Vibrant Red, the handheld features a lightweight silhouette, a knurled aluminium handle and a magnetic docking system that allows it to snap into place.

It’s a milestone for a brand that’s built a multi-million-dollar business around a singular hero product, with distribution spanning Erewhon, Ulta Beauty, Costco, and Target. Jolie is among the cohort of brands that have turned mundane products into premium goods, like Touchland, Native, Blueland and Harry’s before it. That approach extends to Jolie’s creative direction, led by co-founder Arjan Singh, who has brought a fashion point of view and an elevated-yet-cheeky filter to the traditionally utilitarian showerhead category. Rather than relying on product imagery, Jolie’s campaigns focus on the feeling and emotion of showering, an otherwise-intimate daily ritual.

Campaign imagery for the Jolie Filtered Showerhead.

The idea began with a personal discovery, Babenzien says. After noticing his skin was unusually dry one winter, Babenzien, who previously founded direct-to-consumer (DTC) footwear brand Greats before selling it to Steve Madden in 2019, began researching the effects of shower water on skin and hair. His spark moment came in the shower, when he realized that a showerhead could be more than a bathroom fixture: it could become a beauty-wellness essential, the first step in a consumer’s daily routine. “Jolie was my ultimate shower thought to date,” Babenzien says, reflecting on the early days of building the brand.

Now, with years of performance proof behind it, Jolie is ready to expand both its product assortment and its awareness. For Valentine’s Day, Jolie partnered with romance publisher 831 Stories on an Instagram series pairing steamy reads with hot showers. In August, during Copenhagen Fashion Week, Jolie installed showers along the city’s harbor for swimmers, bringing the product into a public setting that combined art with function. It also launched campaign films starring Saturday Night Live cast member Veronika Slowikowska, with a preview airing nationally on NBC around SNL’s 52nd season premiere.

Its editorial series, “Shower Thoughts”, also draws inspiration from the bathroom. Originally a written Q&A, it evolved into a video interview series in October, opening with creative director and designer Alex Eagle. Filmed in and around guests’ bathrooms, the series features creatives with distinct points of view who have built something of their own, reflecting Jolie’s ties to fashion, design, art, and culture. Other first-season guests include Vyrao founder Yasmin Sewell and fashion designer Mara Hoffman.

Creative Director Alex Eagle in Jolie’s Shower Thoughts video series.

Together, the campaigns position the shower as a space for reflection, intimacy, and ritual. “Our brand is our focal point and our competitive advantage,” Babenzien says. Now, he wants to ride that to take over the rest of your water supply.

Jolie, named after Babenzien’s wife and the French word for “pretty”, launched in 2022. Before Jolie could build a brand, it had to make the case for the category itself. “I had conviction. I didn’t have certainty, and there’s a difference.”

From the start, Babenzien identified two challenges: educating consumers on why they should filter their shower water and convincing them they could install the product themselves.

To address the first, Jolie licensed publicly available water-quality data and created a free local water report. Users enter their email address and zip code to receive a breakdown of what is in their water, giving the brand a way to explain the potential impact on skin and hair in seconds.

Jolie calls it “step zero”: filtering shower water to reduce chlorine and other contaminants before applying shampoo, conditioner, or skincare. “Beauty and wellness go hand in hand. It’s not one thing; it’s a sequence of things,” Babenzien explains. “It’s what you eat, where you train, what you put in your body, what you put on your body and how you sleep.”

Hair concerns are the biggest initial purchase driver for Jolie, Babenzien says. While hair shedding and thinning can be linked to stress, hormonal changes and postpartum hair loss, the growing use of GLP-1 medications, which have been associated with hair shedding during rapid weight loss, has brought renewed attention to hair health.

Jolie points to clinical testing of its showerhead, reporting that 81% of study participants experienced reduced hair shedding. Skin concerns, including dryness and irritation, are another part of the brand’s appeal. Jolie says clinical testing showed a 50% improvement in skin dryness after four weeks.

Jolie Filtered Showerhead, in Brushed Gold.

Babenzien had planned to expand Jolie’s assortment sooner, but rapid growth of the original showerhead prompted him to hold off. “We’ve always had a product roadmap,” he says. “We decided not to release other products, because the business was growing so quickly and profitably. It didn’t make sense to complicate our operations and supply chain, or to complicate the proposition for the consumer.”

That focus has paid off. Jolie expects to post between $11 million and $12 million in EBITDA in 2026, and says it has processed two million Shopify orders for showerheads and replacement filters since 2021. The company counts 750,000 “daily active users” — Babenzien’s term for customers who use the showerhead as part of their everyday routine — and aims to reach one million by year-end.

Distribution has gone wide — a sign of a shift in strategy from earlier era DTC brands. Jolie launched on Amazon in June 2022, followed by Erewhon in April 2023, Ulta in January 2025, and Costco US in December 2025. In September 2026, it expanded into 600 Target stores. The brand is also stocked in 2,000 hair salons and says more than 10,000 stylists trust and recommend it. Each retail channel requires a different approach to consumer education, from shower-style end-caps at Erewhon to informational displays around Costco pallets.

And nothing signals a brand’s place in the cultural zeitgeist quite like an Erewhon drink collaboration. Jolie and the retailer first partnered on the Spring of Youth iced elixir in 2025, followed by Sacred Water in July 2026. While the first was positively received, Sacred Water proved more polarizing, drawing criticism online and becoming late-night fodder, including in a Jimmy Kimmel Live segment.

Babenzien views the partnership through a brand rather than a revenue lens. For him, even the polarized response demonstrated Jolie’s ability to generate conversation well beyond the showerhead category.

Erewhon helped establish Jolie’s wellness proposition and introduce the brand to a broader retail audience. “Erewhon is a cultural phenomenon and has national influence across all retail in the US,” Babenzien says.

Antoci adds that demand has remained strong since its debut at Erewhon. “Since Erewhon had never sold a product in this category, we were thrilled to see strong customer demand in the first year, and engagement remains high,” he says.

Word of mouth has been critical to Jolie’s growth, Babenzien says, with packaging designed to make the bathroom fixture feel special. The first 10,000 units included a ceramic disc carrying a bespoke fragrance inspired by the waters of Sicily. The brand discontinued it due to overseas shipping complications, but the attention to detail remains, down to a branded wrench and a custom spool of plumber’s tape. Those tools serve a practical purpose, too: addressing Jolie’s second early obstacle by making installation feel like an approachable DIY task rather than a job for a plumber.

Babenzien says Jolie has generated more than 75,000 pieces of user-generated content, helping the business grow without relying entirely on paid marketing. His broader marketing philosophy centers on the idea that “people influence people”, with the aim of making Jolie a topic of conversation at dinner tables, in hair salons and among running groups.

Jolie showerhead art installation at Ofelia Plads, Copenhagen.

The design presented a different challenge: making an everyday fixture distinctive without allowing it to become trend-driven. The team looked to enduring design references including the Rolex Submariner, the Porsche 911, a black tuxedo and the little black dress. “All of these have evolved over decades, but their design identity is clear,” Babenzien says. Those established design codes now carry through to the handheld, which is immediately recognizable as a Jolie product and boasts the same attention to detail.

Its magnetic mount provides a tactile and audible cue when the showerhead is securely docked, making it easier to put back in place. For Babenzien, the experience of removing and replacing it was as important as its filtration function.

As for further product launches in 2027, Babenzien says: “If it’s related to water as it affects your skin, hair and health, it can live in the current Jolie product roadmap.” Next to launch will be a rainfall showerhead, with non-showerhead innovations to come later down the line.

The company has five full-time employees and has grown without institutional capital, the CEO says. While investors have expressed interest, Jolie is not currently raising capital. He remains open to a partner who could help accelerate its next phase of growth.

For now, Babenzien’s priority is managing that growth while keeping Jolie focused. The company is targeting $100 million in revenue in 2027, up from a projected $65 million in 2026.

“The challenge is in our own hands. We have to remain vigilant and focused on the mission, not lose sight of trying to get everybody to filter their shower water, and hopefully get them to do it with a Jolie.”

Blue whale sightings have fallen off dramatically near the Galápagos. El Niño may be to blame.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For nine months, a scientific expedition searched for blue whales in the waters around the Galápagos Islands but found none. Between October 2025 and July 2026, the researchers surveyed areas of the Ecuadorian archipelago where the giants had historically been recorded, hoping to attach satellite tags and learn more about the animals' migratory routes. The search ended without the team tagging a single whale.

The absence coincided with unusually warm ocean conditions during an El Niño event. Sea surface temperatures were as high as 82 degrees Fahrenheit (28 degrees Celsius), while at a depth of 330 feet (100 meters) water temperatures ranged from 66 to 67 F (18.9 to 19.4 C) — up to 9 F (5 C) warmer than usual for that time of the year.

This raised the possibility that El Niño changed where blue whales were finding food and, in turn, where they went. The researchers suspect the animals may be seeking colder, more productive waters. However, the whales themselves are still missing.

Blue whales have not been feeding off the Galapagos this year, and likely migrated somewhere further south, where waters are cooler and food is more abundant.

"The hypothesis is that the whales are staying in areas with greater productivity [more food] farther south, in waters with slightly cooler temperatures," Daniela Alarcón, the expedition's leader and a researcher at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito's Galápagos campus and the Galápagos Science Center, told Live Science.

As to where the missing whales have gone, possibilities include the waters off Peru and offshore areas where the animals could go undetected. In this scenario, the unusually warm waters around the Galápagos Islands would act as a "temperature barrier," Alarcón said, preventing them from feeding in the archipelago's waters.

Blue whales (Balaenoptera musculus) can consume up to 12,100 pounds (5,500 kilograms) of krill — small crustaceans that make up the whales' primary food source — every day. That means they need to find areas with enough food to sustain them.

"These are very large animals that need to move to areas where they can keep feeding," Alarcón said.

It's not yet clear whether this year's El Niño caused a krill shortage in the waters off the Galápagos, but some indirect evidence points that way.

We thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing.

Past expeditions suggested that blue whales tend to feed in water layers around 71 F, which this season was identified around the Galápagos at a depth of about 197 feet (92 m). By contrast, peak chlorophyll concentrations, an indirect indicator of abundance of the krill's food source, phytoplankton ‪—‬ were recorded much higher in the water column, at between 39 and 121 feet (12 to 37 m) below the surface. Because krill abundance wasn't directly measured, that data suggests, but does not establish, that there was a mismatch between the whales' preferred feeding layer and the presence of their food.

"Honestly, we had never encountered such unusual conditions before," Juan Pablo Muñoz, a marine biologist at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito who was also on the expedition, told Live Science.

The whales' absence did not come as a complete surprise to the team. Sightings had already begun to decline before the most recent expedition. Reports submitted through Cetácea Galápagos, a citizen science network, began to dwindle between August and September 2025. There were two isolated reports of blue whales, in May and June 2026, but the team could not confirm either one, despite intensifying its search.

"We knew conditions wouldn't be the same, but we thought that if we put in more effort, we might be able to find some individuals. But we searched, and searched, and searched — and found nothing," Alarcón recalled.

Despite nine months of looking, a recent expedition to search for blue whales around the Galápagos region did not spot a single one.

Part of that could be down to the elusive nature of the giant creatures. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae)are generally easier to spot, Muñoz noted. In some places, they can be seen from the shore or after a half-hour boat ride. Blue whales, by contrast, rarely approach mainland Ecuador's coast and tend to stay far from populated areas in the Galápagos.

Fernando Félix, a marine biologist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Ecuador who was not part of the expedition, was unsurprised by the result.

"We already knew there wouldn't be any blue whales in the Galápagos," said Félix, who is also a researcher at the Whale Museum (Museo de Ballenas).

Félix told Live Science that there are historical precedents for this behavior in the southeastern Pacific. During the 1982-1983 El Niño, which also brought substantial ocean warming, blue whales and other species, including fin whales (Balaenoptera physalus) and Bryde's whales (Balaenoptera brydei), were recorded shifting southward.

"We might think that because they are 'just animals,' they lack memory or don't understand these processes — but we would be wrong," Félix said. "They can clearly sense that when temperatures are unusually high as they travel north from the south, vertical mixing has been disrupted and there is no food in the Galápagos. They perceive environmental conditions and naturally direct their movements toward areas where they believe feeding conditions are better."

Sea surface and subsurface temperatures during the 2015 El Niño, showing a band of warmer water at depth. After that season, whale sightings bounced back, suggesting the missing blue whales will return once water conditions cool.

Rather than indicating a mass die-off, the whales' disappearance may reflect a shift in their movements in response to changing ocean conditions, Félix said.

"I don't think the whales have died," Felix said. "They simply didn't go to the Galápagos region. They went elsewhere, where conditions were better."

This response to environmental conditions may also have impacted dolphin movements. Pods may have moved toward colder waters, where food could be more abundant, or may have even dispersed, Félix suggested.

El Niño's effects will likely persist over the coming months. "Between January and May 2027, we'll have warm water coming from the north and warm water coming from the west," Félix warned. "This is going to hit us extremely hard."

Blue whales, humpback whales and dolphins would likely return to Galápagos waters once El Niño subsides and ocean conditions begin to normalize. He said pelagic fish (species that live in the water column rather than on or near the seafloor) ‪—‬ including tuna, swordfish, anchovies and sardines, which have also moved toward colder waters ‪—‬ would return as well.

Muñoz agreed. Krill populations can rebound just one to three months after cold, nutrient-rich waters begin to rise to the surface. More whale sightings were recorded in the years following the 2015 and 2023 El Niño events. Based on these precedents, he suggested that 2028 could be a promising year if cold water returns to the surface. "The system bounces back," he said.

Félix compared El Niño to a computer restart. "It resets the environment, allowing ecological processes to begin again," he said. He's confident that blue whales will return to the area. "I can guarantee that there will be large numbers of blue whales at this time in 2028," he told Live Science.

#6580. Japanese Sweet Potato Chaat

Every cuisine has a sauce that’s an absolute essential—a ride or die, if you will. For South Asian food, this is a cilantro mint green chutney. It brings a punchy, herb-packed burst of flavor that goes with pretty much everything. This recipe combines cilantro, mint, and just the right amount of heat from green chiles, creating a balance of spice and freshness. Lime juice adds brightness, while cumin, sugar, and chaat masala add complexity. Use this as a zesty topping for your favorite dish or as a base for pani puri water (just add 1½ cups [360 ml] of water and strain), or make it creamy with yogurt or sour cream to use for spreading and dipping.

Slow-roasting Japanese sweet potatoes flesh-side down releases their natural sugars, caramelizing and deepening their sweetness. The flesh becomes incredibly tender, almost custard-like in texture, while the skin turns a rich golden brown and becomes slightly crispy. So don’t bother peeling them! Top them with tamarind concentrate (I like Tamicon, Cock Brand, Pure Indian Foods, or Dragonfly—anything without citric acid), green chutney, fresh onions, tomatoes, and cilantro for a chaat-inspired appetizer.

To a blender or food processor, add 2 bunches cilantro (about 6 oz. [170 g]), leaves and stems, 1 bunch mint (about 2 oz. [55 g]), leaves and tender stems, 6 green Thai chiles or 2 serranos, stemmed (more if you want it spicier), ½ cup (120 ml) lime juice (from about 5 limes), 2 tsp. cumin seeds, 1½ tsp. fine sea salt, 1 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. chaat masala. Pulse for a few seconds in intervals until the ingredients are pulverized into a smooth paste. Transfer to an airtight container and store until ready to use, up to 1 week in the refrigerator or 1 month in the freezer.

Preheat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and line a baking sheet with parchment paper.

Drizzle the sheet with extra-virgin olive oil and place 1½ lb. (680 g) Japanese or Korean sweet potatoes, ends trimmed, halved lengthwise, cut-side down. Bake for 60 to 70 minutes, until golden and caramelized on the cut side and cooked through and tender; a knife inserted into the center of the potato should slide through easily. Let rest for 5 to 8 minutes. Once cool enough to handle, cut the sweet potatoes into 1" to 2" [2.5 to 5 cm] pieces.

To a small bowl, add ½ cup (120 g) plain whole-milk yogurt or sour cream and ½ tsp. fine sea salt and whisk to combine. If you’re using sour cream, thin it out with a little water.

Place the sweet potatoes on a serving platter and drizzle the yogurt, ½ cup Evergreen Chutney, 3 Tbsp. tamarind concentrate or paste, and 2 Tbsp. lime juice evenly all over. Sprinkle with 1 medium red tomato (5 oz. [140 g]), finely chopped, 1 small red onion (7 oz. [200 g]), finely chopped, 2 Tbsp. chopped cilantro leaves and tender stems, 1 tsp. chaat masala, 3 green Thai chiles or 1 serrano, stemmed, thinly sliced, and crispy sev and serve immediately.

Do Ahead: You can make the individual components a day ahead of time and store them in airtight containers in the refrigerator, then assemble to serve.

#6578. Hidden in the Viral Last Ditch Debacle: How to Keep Lesbian Bars Alive

By September of this year, Jackie Matellian had spent months living in her truck while working several jobs to keep Last Ditch, a lesbian bar in Greenfield, Massachusetts, open. She was the last remaining original founder, and the bar was in deep financial trouble. According to reporting by The Boston Globe, workers had gone unpaid, Matellian was carrying a $50,000 start-up loan, and the landlord wanted $3,900 in overdue rent.

Last Ditch had been built to do things most bars don’t even attempt. It welcomed lesbians, transsexuals, and other queer people who couldn’t afford the cover, offered a free store with food, clothing and harm-reduction supplies, and required KN95 masks or better. For immunocompromised patrons, those precautions made it possible to have a night out without gambling with their health. The bar’s radical inclusiveness was part of why people cared about it—and part of what its owners were struggling to finance it.

Desperate for cash, the bar’s management announced a policy shift with a cheery Instagram post: Saturday nights would become mask-optional. The gamble backfired. By treating accessibility as negotiable, the bar alienated immunocompromised regulars without attracting enough new customers to pay the rent. Follow-up stumbles culminated in a marathon three-and-a-half-hour community meeting that collapsed without a resolution. Rather than saving the venue, the policy pivot left Last Ditch with the worst of both worlds: fractured community trust and an unresolved financial crisis.

The drama became national entertainment, right up until October 26, when Last Ditch announced its soft closure.

The spectators moved on, but one issue remains: expecting one struggling lesbian bar to compensate for the failures of an entire social infrastructure is absurd. The irony is that Western Massachusetts built the blueprint for combating exactly this.

Women in the area have been finding ways to share the costs of lesbian social life for decades. UMass Amherst documents more than 400 lesbian and feminist groups active in the region between 1968 and 1978. Northampton had the Common Womon Club, Lesbian Gardens, Womonfyre Books, and the Nutcracker’s Suite self-defense dojo. These were places women built to make their social lives and organizing possible outside institutions that routinely excluded them.

In 1976, the women behind Common Womon pooled money to buy property through Ceres Inc., the nonprofit they’d formed, then financed renovations with help from donations and a loan. The adjacent storefront provided rental income and housed the Nutcracker’s Suite, then Womonfyre Books, so control of the property also gave the women a way to make room for other projects and help pay for the place they shared. Common Womon also collected sliding-scale membership dues, while the Valley Women’s History Collaborative lists benefits for the Common Womon Club that helped keep it going.

The womon-spelling and the names are fun to inherit; I also want us to inherit the ability to put actual premises under our control. For Last Ditch, that begins with finding out whether a new set of owners can remain in the building on terms the business can afford.

Matellian had already told the Globe she planned to turn the bar into a cooperative. For that to relieve the pressure on her, new members would need to take responsibility for work she’d been doing and agree on how the existing debt would be handled. But calling it a cooperative wouldn’t do much for Matellian if she was still the person everyone called whenever something went wrong. Sharing authority has to include sharing responsibility for the work, with limits on what any one person is expected to carry.

Sharing ownership would give people more power over decisions and occasions to disagree about them. Common Womon closed in 1982, while Womonfyre lasted until 1989. Womonfyre faced harassment and threats from outside the lesbian community as well as conflicts over sexual politics and what the shop should sell. Its archive preserves those disputes alongside bank statements and instructions for running the store.

A cooperative at Last Ditch would need procedures for making decisions in tandem with conflict resolution. Which is why I like that the Womonfyre archive makes room for instructions on running the shop alongside political disputes. A disagreement over how to run a bar doesn’t become abuse because people are arguing. Treating every conflict as a verdict on someone’s character makes it harder to agree on a change, because the argument can continue long after the conduct has stopped or the policy has been reversed.

Making that possible at Last Ditch requires paid training and a written account of all this work. A cooperative whose members can debate the mission for four hours but can’t cover a shift or pay its debt will end up crushing the same woman behind the bar.

If Last Ditch is to survive, its next incarnation must trade endless character trials for operational infrastructure: shared labor, transparent books, and creative financing strategies.

If one thing the Globe’s reporting revealed, it is that one commercial bar bearing the weight of an entire community’s social safety crushes everyone under impossible expectations. Instead, we must look for ways to anchor the politics in practical economics, share the burden, and build a room strong enough to hold the argument without tearing down the house.

Anyone asking the community to save Last Ditch needs to be prepared to share control of what survives.
